div.head: List of papers by countries
div.p: [Incoming papers are listed chronologically under date of issue. Unless otherwise specified, the correspondence is from or to the Secretary of State or the Department. Correspondence to and from the London Office of the Commission for Relief in Belgium sent through the American Ambassador in London, is listed under Great Britain.]

row.cell: Argentine attitude toward Germany theoretically at one with that of the United States, but, in absence of concrete injury, form of reply will appear different.
Forwards copy of Argentina’s reply to Germany deploring extreme measures of blockade and declaring adherence to rules of international law.
Argentine initiative in suggesting that Latin-American powers mediate between Germany and the United States.
Probable outcome or projected Latin-American conference.
Announces the arming of U.S. merchant ships.
Instructions to report Argentina’s activities regarding mediation by Latin-American powers.
Slight activity in promoting move for Latin-American mediation.
Quotes Argentine note recognizing justice of U.S. action against Germany.
From President Irigoyen of Argentina to the American Ambassador
Recognition of justice of U.S. action against Germany.
Sinking of the Argentine brigantine Monte Protegido by German submarine may cause severance of diplomatic relations.
Argentina expresses appreciation of attitude of Brazil in defense of principles of international law.
Calling of commercial conference of American nations at Argentina includes the United States.
Quotes proposed Argentine invitation to the nations of America.
Inquiry regarding message of Mar. 16, 6 p.m., on commercial congress.
Changes in title of congress of American nations to be called by Argentina.
Inquires U.S. attitude relative to conference of neutral American nations.
Quotes text of Argentine note of invitation to nations of America for conference to procure mutual understanding on the war
Impossibility of any expression of views by the United States regarding conference of Latin-American nations.
Press reports that Argentina demands apology and indemnity of Germany for sinking of brigantine.
Attempt of Argentina to interpret the meaning of U.S. reply regarding proposed conference of American nations.
Socialist Party voted against intervention in the war.
Reported that Germany has agreed to indemnify Argentina for loss of vessel and will salute Argentine flag.
Argentina accepts German promise of reparation, ratifying friendly sentiments between the two countries.
Presents Argentine message explaining move for congress of American nations and desire to remove any misunderstanding regarding friendly relations with the United States.
British safe-conduct granted German Minister to Brazil to proceed to Germany. Inquiry regarding U.S. safe-conduct to New York.
Authorization to issue safe-conduct to former German Minister. Right of search reserved.
Peru consents to join conference only on condition that it act under leadership of the United States.
Reports countries which will participate in conference of neutrals.
Annual message to Congress recites Argentina’s efforts to maintain neutrality and plan for congress of neutrals.
Request for outline of plan of congress of neutrals.
Date and program of conference uncertain. Believed that Argentina’s note to Germany will result in severance of diplomatic relations.
Inquires if Argentina can assist the United States in its plan of export allotment to the Allies by sending more wheat to France and Great Britain unconditionally.
Colombia and Mexico most active in urging congress of neutrals.
Argentina will declare war if demands not accepted by Germany.
German reply to Argentine demands considered acceptable.
Quotes three messages from Luxburg, German Chargé in Argentina, to Berlin, dispatched as official messages of Swedish Legation and recommending drastic treatment of Argentine ships.
Revocation or Argentine export-prohibition decree urged. Attempted adjustment.
Publishing of Department’s communiqué on Luxburg’s messages to Berlin. Swedish Minister denies having sent them.
Foreign Minister denies any undertakings for limiting of Argentine shipping; awaits official confirmation before taking action on Luxburg messages.
Reported German Chargé has been given his passports.
Report requested on interned German vessels, also on Argentine merchant vessels.
Argentine merchant marine and their whereabouts.
Argentine Senate voted to break relations with Germany.
All cables sent by Swedish Legation transmitted to Argentine Ambassador at Washington.
German Government disavows Luxburg messages. Argentina undecided regarding future attitude toward Germany.
Reported House votes rupture of diplomatic relations with Germany.
Details of House vote on severance of relations with Germany.
Instructions to deny that information published regarding German despatches at Department for decoding came from the U.S. Government.
Certain countries respond to Argentina’s urge for conference. Brazil excluded.
Proposed purchase of Argentine surplus wheat by British and French; U.S. cooperation in plan.
Conference with the President on Argentina’s international policy. Invitation to Pan-American conference would be tendered if the United States
Instructions to deny rumor that the United States and Great Britain approve the Pope’s further mediation in war.
Understood that Peru, Bolivia, and Uruguay will not be represented at conference unless called for purpose of breaking relations with Germany.
Quotes message to the Treasury from commissioner at Paris that France and Great Britain favor acquiring supplies in Argentina on open market. The United States has like policy.
Instructions regarding U.S. attitude toward the conference. Stand taken by Latin-American countries.
The President determined not to break with Germany. Luxburg telegrams said to be work of madman.
More Luxuurg telegrams published. Government disavows contents.
Informed that proposed congress of neutrals postponed. Instructions to report.
Instructions to deny, if advisable, that the Washington Post voices views of the administration.
General opinion that Latin-American conference will never take place.
Text of proposed convention between France, Great Britain, and Argentina for purchase of wheat in exchange for combustibles from the United States. Requests instructions.
The United States would allow export of combustibles for Argentine requirements, but considers it inadvisable to make engagement.
Argentina will accept wheat convention if U.S. position regarding coal stated definitely. Submits statement on subject for approval.
Authorization to send to Foreign Minister note regarding coal export as submitted for approval.
Convention for the purchase of Argentine wheat by Great Britain and France signed.
Instructions to deny press report that the President will send second peace note to the powers.
Quotes Austria-Hungary’s counter-reply to Allies’ rejection of Central powers’ invitation to discuss peace.
Favorable reception given the President’s peace address by Minister President of Hungary.
From the Hungarian Minister President to the American Ambassador
Attitude toward President Wilson’s peace address.
Quotes note of Jan. 25 from the Hungarian Minister President.
From the Austro-Hungarian Minister of Foreign Affairs to the American Ambassador
Announces resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare.
Text of the President’s address of Feb. 3 to Congress, for the Foreign Minister and for publication.
Efforts or Austro-Hungarian Ambassador designate to continue diplomatic relations with the United States.
Foreign Minister desires that good relations between the United States and Austria-Hungary be maintained.
Quotes Foreign Minister’s note appealing to the President.
From the Austro-Hungarian Minister of Foreign Affairs
Appeal to the President to induce the Entente to conform to American viewpoint and conclude peace honorable to both sides.
Report on the Monarchy’s desperate situation and desire for peace.
Message for transmission from the Bulgarian Minister at Washington to his Government, stating the United States desires to maintain friendly relations with Bulgaria.
The Kaiser expected in Vienna for conference with the Emperor.
Uncertainty of interpretation of Austria-Hungary’s declarations on submarine warfare. Instructions to ascertain attitude.
Austria-Hungary taking precautions against break with America. No submarine activity outside the Adriatic.
Drastic measures to prevent press articles hostile to America.
Offer to Austria-Hungary of Allies’ limited assurances against dismemberment in the event of a request for early peace.
Austria-Hungary must change its submarine policy, otherwise its representative can not be received by the United states
Foreign Minister gives assurance of satisfactory reply to communication regarding the Ancona and persia pledges.
Official denial that the Lyman M. Law was sunk by Austro-Hungarians.
Quotes Austro-Hungarian Foreign Minister’s memorandum refusing to consider separate peace.
From the Austro-Hungarian Minister of Foreign Affairs to the American Ambassador
Official assurance of satisfactory reply to U.S. inquiry regarding submarine warfare.
Quotes Austria-Hungary’s justification of submarine policy.
From the Austro-Hungarian Foreign Office to the American Embassy
Instructions to request reconsideration of separate peace; delay may make it ineffective.
Foreign Minister requests that full reception be given the Ambassador designate in the United States.
Difficulty in handling Austro-Hungarian relief work in Russia separate from that of Germany. Inquires if desired that American Embassy continue its representation.
Austria-Hungary continues to refuse consideration of separate peace.
Prospect of difficulties if Austro-Hungarian Ambassador designate not received in Washington.
U.S. position regarding official reception of Austro-Hungarian Ambassador designate.
From the Austro-Hungarian Minister of Foreign Affairs to the American Ambassador
Requests continuation of U.S. protection in Russia.
U.S. delay in receiving the Austro-Hungarian Ambassador designate.
Refusal to receive Ambassador designate and offer of safe-conduct to Vienna. Instructions for U. S. Ambassador to report in Washington.
Austria-Hungary will sever diplomatic relations with the United States if latter declares war on Germany.
Relations between the United States and Austria-Hungary severed. Guaranty for safe return of personnel of Embassy and consulates requested.
Passports for Austro-Hungarian official party granted.
Austro-Hungarian Chargé has requested passports. Instructions to transfer U.S. and Allied interests to neutral governments.
Austro-Hungarian request for protective measures for officials departing from the United States. Embassy’s reply.
Inquiry whether deportations continue and what percentage of those deported are being returned.
Further report on Belgian deportations and efforts to influence the situation.
From the Belgian Minister for Foreign Affairs to the American Ambassador in France
Belgian note accompanying Allies’ reply to the President’s peace note.
Reports milder methods of deportation and attempt of civil government to abrogate policy.
Change of methods of deportation in Brussels. Encloses summons blank.
From the Minister in Belgium (tel.): for the President
Suggests intervention in order that British and German restrictions on shipping will not destroy Belgian relief work.
Arrangements to be made in event Germany desires withdrawal of American Minister from Belgium.
Instructions to represent to German authorities that their trade restrictions have cut off Belgian relief ships.
Instructions to inform German authorities that unless American Minister and relief commission be accorded former privileges, they will be withdrawn.
Reports status of Legation and relief commission and recommends preparation for gradual departure.
The commission is instructed to remain. Difficulty is divergence of opinion between Great Britain and Germany regarding shipping routes.
Desirable that Minister remain for present. Recommends Hoover’s plan to transfer relief work to Netherland subjects, if Americans must withdraw
Instructions to advise Americans to leave Belgium and to facilitate their departure.
German authorities accord every privilege except diplomatic recognition; will withdraw from occupied territory.
Attempt to put into effect suggestion for reorganization of commission. Only oral assurances given that commission can depart when they desire.
Instructions not to leave Belgium until directed. Commission to depart at same time.
Instructions to obtain written assurances from German authorities that American members of commission may leave Belgium when they desire.
Recommends early departure of commission; the Netherlands and Spain agree to conduct relief in Belgium.
Belgian relief work will cease only when Americans are forced out.
Secured written assurances that members of American commission may leave Belgium in case of war, but subject to quarantine measures.
Orders withdrawal of American Minister and relief workers from Belgium.
From the Minister formerly in Belgium (tel.)
Reports departure from Belgium of Legation staff, consuls, and relief commission with few exceptions.
Bolivia in accord with U.S. view on Germany’s submarine policy.
Quotes Bolivian note to Germany stating Bolivia unites with the United States in protesting against restriction of neutral shipping.
U.S. appreciation of Bolivia’s supporting attitude in severing relations with Germany.
Bolivia declines to participate in conference.
From the Brazilian Minister for Foreign Affairs to the American Chargé
Concurs in pacific sentiments expressed by the President’s peace note.
Brazil will protest against German policy; looks to concerted action of South American powers; and supports action of the United States.
From the Brazilian Minister for Foreign Affairs to the American Chargé
Brazil has protested against German blockade and will hold Germany responsible for incidents resulting therefrom.
Quotes in part Brazil’s note of Feb. 8.
Severance of relations with Germany by Brazil in consequence of the sinking of the Paraná.
From the Consul General at Rio de Janeiro (tel.)
Brazil takes possession of German shipping in its ports.
Foreign Minister requests that voyage of German official party leaving Brazil be unimpeded.
Instructions issued against molestation of former German Minister to Brazil and party on voyage.
No recourse left Brazil and the United States but to take up arms to meet attacks on neutral shipping.
Decreed that Brazil comply with neutrality rules of 1914 until further orders to the contrary.
Intimation that, if satisfactory cooperation with the United States can be effected, Brazil will revoke neutrality decree.
Text of message of President of Brazil to Congress on foreign policy.
Quotes text of the Brazilian President’s message to Congress recommending appropriation of German merchant ships in Brazilian ports.
Brazilian Chamber of Deputies passed resolution authorizing withdrawal of decree of neutrality as affecting the United States and Germany.
Foreign Relations Committee of Brazilian Chamber recommends appropriation of German merchant vessels and takes measures for defense of foreign commerce.
Bill passed revoking decree of neutrality in war between the United States and Germany and authorizing use of German interned vessels.
Brazil unwilling to revoke neutrality decrees affecting Allies until England removes prohibition on Brazilian coffee to Great Britain. U. S. good offices desired.
Brazil appropriates German vessels anchored in Brazilian ports.
Unalterable friendship of Brazil for the United States and policy of continental solidarity.
Quotes President Wilson’s message of appreciation of Brazil’s move.
Inquiry regarding safe-conducts for other members of German Embassy party and for German Minister formerly in Bolivia.
Authorizes granting of safe-conduct to members of German party not already taken care of and to German Minister formerly in Bolivia. Why will Frisia stop at New York?
Reports sailing of Frisia with German Minister and official party; will touch at New York to discharge passengers and cargo.
Appreciation of friendly cooperation of Brazil in U. S. war policy.
Revocation of Brazil’s neutrality decree with respect to Allied powers.
From the Brazilian Minister for Foreign Affairs to the American Ambassador
British conditions regarding shipments of coffee to Great Britain unacceptable to Brazil. Patrol of Brazilian coast.
Brazilian Navy will cooperate with U.S. Navy in patrolling South Atlantic.
Brazilian coast patrol and Allied patrol of high seas.
France secures tonnage from Brazilian company; consideration, purchase of coffee. Suggests negotiations with this company.
Proposition to secure interned German vessels from Brazil by cash payment or fair exchange after war.
Conference with President Braz on German ship proposition.
Urges acceptance of U.S. proposal to take over German merchant vessels.
Probable Brazil will propose that ex-German ships shall be chartered to the United States, France, and Great Britain for their common interest.
Suggestion that offer be made first to the United States to charter ex-German ships, in adherence to doctrines of Americanism.
U.S. and French proposals for extending Brazil’s foreign commerce and assisting the cause of the Allies by employing ex-German vessels.
Brazil’s plan for use of ex-German ships.
Brazilian mission to the United States.
Every possible facility will be extended to Brazilian commission.
Quotes the Brazilian President’s message to Congress relating to sinking of S.S. Mação and recommending war with Germany.
France unwilling to withdraw proposal for acquisition of German ships in Brazil.
Quotes Brazilian Senate resolutions declaring war with Germany.
From President Wilson to President Braz of Brazil (tel.)
Brazil’s entrance into war welcomed by the United States and associated nations.
The President suggests that the United States stand aside and let France negotiate for Brazilian ships.
Argentina proposes a congress of Latin-Americans rather than a congress of neutrals. Brazil and Uruguay have inquired program.
Great Britain refuses to relax restrictions on coffee from Brazil, Imports confined to necessities.
Brazil wishes to prevent Latin-American conference or to impose condition that attendance depend upon breaking relations with Germany.
Charter to France of German ships seized by Brazil.
Instructions to report whether, under French and Brazilian agreement, any North Atlantic trade is intended.
Brazil’s request for U.S. naval officers and offer to send squadron to Mediterranean. Ambassador recommends invitation be extended to join American squadron.
Invitation for Brazilian squadron to join American naval forces; naval officers will be furnished as requested.
Trade arrangement between France and Brazil will benefit France. No provision for use of ships in North Atlantic.
Inquires if vessels not chartered by France are available for charter by the United States through shipping Board.
France secured best ex-German vessels. Remainder not available or desirable for charter to the United States.
From the Bulgarian Minister of Foreign Affairs to the American Consul General at Sofia
Situation created by Entente refusal to accept peace proposals.
From the Consul General at Sofia
To the Consul General at Sofia (tel.)
Instructions to suggest continuance of friendly relations between the United States and Bulgaria.
From the Consul General at Sofia (tel.)
Bulgaria reciprocates friendly feelings of the United States.
From the Consul General at Sofia (tel.)
Bulgaria intends to preserve friendly relations with the United States.
Chile in note to Germany refuses acceptance of blockade measure and reserves rights.
Quotes in part Chile’s note disclosing unity of purpose with the United States in favor of general rights of neutrality.
From the Chilean Minister for Foreign Affairs to the American Ambassador
Chile’s unity of purpose with the United States in favor of general rights of neutrality.
Instructions to report, on activities of Argentina regarding mediation by Latin-American powers, also on attitude of Chile.
Chile and Brazil will not join Argentine movement for mediation between the United States and Germany.
Presents copy of Chile’s note to Brazil commending action of latter in repealing neutrality decree.
Interview with Chilean Ambassador regarding Chile’s war policy.
Possibility of Chile’s alignment with Brazil and the United States.
Evidence of change in Chilean neutrality policy. U.S. Fleet would be received as friendly visitor.
Chile wishes to pursue neutral policy until directly wronged. If American Fleet reaches Pacific, would receive it in friendly spirit.
Appreciation of Chile’s friendly attitude. Not known when fleet will reach Pacific.
Copy of Chilean telegram of Nov. 9 quoting message to Argentina inquiring object of proposed congress.
Quotes Foreign Minister’s approval of President Wilson’s peace note of Dec. 18, 1916.
From the Chinese Minister for Foreign Affairs to the American Minister
Approval of President Wilson’s peace note of Dec. 18, 1916.
China requests assurances on certain points in event of severing relations with Germany.
China will probably associate itself with American action if certain assurances are given by the United States.
China fearful lest Japan secure mandate to supervise Chinese military organization. Quotes assurances of U.S. assistance, which he proposes to make.
China has protested to Germany against measures of blockade; if protest ineffectual, relations will be severed.
Instructions to give no further assurances of support to China at present. Matter under consideration.
Inability to give assurances of support to China. Warning against isolated action.
Will take no action until further 408 instructed. Suggestion that U.S. leadership could prevent unilateral action harmful to China.
Résumé of steps taken and argument used in urging China to associate itself with policy and action of the United States.
China should not do more than break diplomatic relations with Germany until U.S. decision is reached.
The United States not disposed to urge China to declare war on Germany. Recommends awaiting developments.
Japan bringing strong pressure to bear to force China to join Allies.
Japanese pressure, internal politics, Allied financial assurances, and failure of the United States to give assistance, all tend to induce China to join the Allies.
Informed of China’s overtures to join Entente powers in return for certain assistance. Instructions to recommend that China wait.
Discussion of China’s alignment with either the United States or the Allies. Latter offer inducements.
China sees advantage in joining Allies. Early determination of attitude by the United States necessary.
Events and influences in China prior to break in relations with Germany.
Parliament votes break in relations with Germany. American International Corp. causes distrust of the United States.
The United States not in position to give practical assurances to China, but will lend influence for its welfare.
Instructions to inform China that declaration of war inadvisable; internal discord deprecated.
Severance of relations with Germany by China.
From the Consul General at Canton to the Minister in China
Report on attitude in southern China toward war with Germany.
Germany willing to discuss safeguarding lives and property of Chinese but refuses to renounce submarine methods. Relations severed.
Enumeration or China’s desires. Attitude of the United States.
U. S. attitude toward China remains unchanged.
China’s desires will receive consideration under certain conditions enumerated.
Report of situation in China after break in relations with Germany. Enclosure: Consular report of Mar. 16 from Canton.
China wishes to be informed of American action respecting Germany before further decision made as to policy.
Advantages to be derived from China’s entrance into the war. Inclined to follow American policy.
Summary of development of diplomatic situation after protest to Germany.
Possibility or Financial assistance to China through congressional appropriation for loans.
Recommends that indication of financial assistance to China be withheld until methods and conditions decided upon.
U.S. situation regarding financial assistance to China.
Requests to be informed of any statements made to Chinese Minister regarding financial assistance.
Chinese Minister was told that China, if at war with Germany, had reason to expect financial assistance under bill pending in Congress. Text of bill quoted.
Requests that he be informed upon passage of bill for financial assistance, before signature by the President.
China on verge of declaration of war. Inquires if possible to extend financial assistance to equip reserves, etc.
Bill for financial assistance already signed by the President. Action delayed because interpretation must be decided by the Department of Justice.
Diplomatic situation and question whether China is to declare war against Germany. Enclosure: Memorandum of conversation with the Premier
Inquires regarding U.S. cooperation in protection of Mukden Railway zone by foreign troops to exclusion of Chinese troops.
The United States declines to change its attitude toward question of excluding Chinese troops from Tientsin.
Criticism of article published in the Saturday Evening Post on action taken by China against Germany.
Suggests mission to China to forestall action adverse to Chinese independence and American interests.
Suggested mission would accord with expectations of China to complete invitation to sever relations with Germany.
Assurances of Allies in connection with impending declaration of war by China. Instructions requested.
Character of China’s participation in war should be decided after consultation with Allies.
Authorization to offer to China, after declaration of war is made, assurances similar to those proposed by the Allies.
Quotes Chinese note announcing declaration of war with Germany and Austria-Hungary.
From the Chinese Foreign Office to the American Legation
Announces declaration of war with Germany and Austria-Hungary.
Efforts to secure Allied assurance of cooperation in maintaining Chinese sovereignty.
Approval of Colombian treaty desired. Apprehension lest the United States invade Colombia to protect canal in case of war.
From the Minister in Costa Rica (tel.)
Costa Rica will observe benevolent neutrality and try to prevent development of hostility against the United States within its territory.
To the Minister in Costa Rica via Salvador
Guatemala’s action in severing relations with Germany and offering support to the United states.
From the Chargé in Costa Rica (tel.)
De facto Government of Costa Rica would sever relations with Germany in case of U.S. recognition.
From the Chargé in Costa Rica (tel.)
Move of Costa Rican de facto Government to sever relations with Germany irrespective of recognition. Safe-conduct for German Charge requested.
To the Chargé in Costa Rica (tel.)
Safe-conduct will be granted German representative, when requested by neutral state, so far as it concerns U.S. forces.
From the Chargé in Costa Rica (tel.)
Severance of relations with Germany by the Tinoco Government in Costa Rica.
From the Chargé in Costa Rica (tel.)
Safe-conducts for German representative in Costa Rica issued.
Cuba ready to render moral and material support to the United States against Germany.
Cuban protest against German note on submarine warfare, opening way for severance of relations.
Message from the Foreign Minister stating Cuba identified with the United States in policy; Cuban President will request authorization to declare a state of war with Germany.
Quotes text of act authorizing the the Cuban President to declare war on Germany.
Commission to be sent to Washington to confer regarding Cuba’s part in war. Precautions taken on land and in harbor
President Wilson’s message to the President of Cuba in appreciation of Cuba’s declaration of war against Germany.
Gratification at Cuba’s desire to cooperate by sending commission to the United States.
Proposal that Cuba requisition German vessels and dispose of them to the United States. Suggested method of procedure.
Cuba will not sell German prize vessels but offers use of them to the United States on any terms desired.
Arrangements proposed for use by the United States of ex-German vessels.
Arrangements for remuneration when Cuba turns over ex-German ships to U.S. Shipping Board.
German interned ships in Cuba to be turned over to him as agent of Shipping Board.
Four German steamships, prizes of war, transferred to U.S. Shipping Board.
Formalities of law regarding registry of German merchant vessels seized by Cuba and turned over to the United States.
U.S. proposals for chartering German ships seized by Cuba.
Declaration of war on Austria-Hungary by Cuba.
The President seeking legal way to conform with Shipping Board’s proposals for chartering ex-German vessels.
Quotes Denmark’s note declining to follow the United States in severing relations with Germany.
From the Danish Minister of Foreign Affairs to the American Minister
Denmark declines to follow the the United States in severing relations with Germany.
Instructions to report whether Danish Government prohibits entrance and departure of merchant vessels armed for defensive purposes.
German Socialist leader reported as urging that bill be introduced before Reichstag granting equal suffrage in electing its members
Denmark wishes to preserve its neutrality. Neither British nor French armed vessels have entered its ports.
Quotes German Foreign Minister’s address before the Reichstag in justification of his overtures to Mexico.
Press report of German Chancellor’s speech concerning possibility of war with the United States.
Austria-Hungary advocates peace conference and opposes an armistice.
substance of message reported sent to Duma by German Socialists congratulating Russian proletariat on political progress.
Quotes and comments on Ecuador’s reply to U.S. suggestion that neutrals sever relations with Germany.
From the Ecuadoran Minister for Foreign Affairs to the American Minister
Reply to U.S. suggestion that neutrals sever relations with Germany.
Presents Ecuador’s proposal of an American Congress for agreeing upon joint action to protect neutral rights.
Ecuador accepts invitation to conference; continues neutrality.
From the Ecuadoran Minister for Foreign Affairs
Ecuador favors a congress for promotion of Pan-American understanding.
Presents Foreign Office note and memorandum of Sept. 11.
To the Ecuadoran Minister for Foreign Affairs
Acknowledges Ecuadoran note of Sept. 11 recommending a continental policy for defense of American interests.
Ecuador will attend Latin-American congress if all American countries previously reach common agreement.
Severance of relations with Germany by Ecuador.
Ecuador offers its waters and wireless stations to friendly war vessels without restriction.
Instructions to suspend activities in behalf of Germany until the country taking over German interests is indicated.
Germany has intrusted its interests in the United States and all belligerent countries to Switzerland, except in Russia where Sweden has charge.
Application for establishment of Serbian Legation in the United States, designating minister under consideration.
A Serbian diplomatic mission under minister proposed will be agreeable to the United States.
Inquiry regarding reports that commissions in the Navy are being issued to commanders of French Line vessels.
From the Consul General at Paris
Additional list of absolute contraband announced.
Commissions in the Navy have not been issued to merchant marine officers.
Instructions to deny press report that the President will send second peace note to the powers.
Questions the purpose of armament on merchant vessels. Case of the French S.S. Mississippi.
Allies’ reply to the President’s peace note received, also separate note from Belgium.
Quotes Allies reply to the President’s peace note and a separate Belgian note.
From the Consul General at Marseilles
Sinking of the British S.S. Mohacsfield.
The President’s Senate address endorsed by French Socialist Party and press. Latter holds that peace should come only after victory of Allies.
Instructions to suspend activities in behalf of Germany until the country taking over German interests is indicated.
Requests safe-conduct and facilities for German representatives and families leaving the United States.
Requests safe-conduct for German party to sail on the Frederik VIII. Inquires if vessel may carry other passengers and cargo.
Safe-conduct accorded German Ambassador and party.
Germany has intrusted its interests in the United States and all belligerent countries to Switzerland, except in Russia where Sweden has charge.
No objection to other German passengers embarking on the Frederik VIII with German official party.
Sinking of Danish S.S. Lars Kruse with cargo of corn for Belgian relief.
Attack upon and escape of British ship Wallace.
France willing to expedite dispatch of pouches marked “Shipping Documents” if the United States gives assurance that they contain only such papers.
Quotes inquiries received at U.S. Post Office regarding detention of mail for neutral countries.
Inquiry regarding interference with commercial mail for Greece.
Unable to give guaranties for contents of pouches marked “Shipping Documents”
From the Consul General at Marseilles
Attack on British merchant steamer Corso.
From the Consul at La Rochelle (tel.)
From the Counselor for the Department of State to the French Ambassador
Treasury instructions issued to omit name of port of destination from export declarations if country of destination is given.
From the Consul General at Marseilles (tel.)
Explanation offered for non-delivery of U. S. commercial letters for Greece.
Sinking of the American S.S. Aztec.
French cooperation requested to facilitate departure from the United States of Austro-Hungarian Embassy and consular officers, together with German officials from China.
Advisable for Liberia to sever relations with Germany if Great Britain and France will give temporary protection.
French safe-conduct granted steamer carrying Austro-Hungarian staff and German consuls from China.

Deportation of Germans and resumption of trade with Liberia.
Efforts to induce the United States to join Allies in urging Siam to break relations with Germany. Advantages of such move.
Declines to make further suggestions to Siam concerning relations with Germany.
Disposition of mail matter detained in France.
French notification that correspondence marked “Shipping Documents” shall be examined and dispatched to destination.
Approval of Liberian arrangements for deporting German officials, women, and children.
No objection to Liberian plan for deporting German officials, women, and children.
Uruguay not inclined to give the French and British the freedom of its ports. Instructions to suggest that matter be dropped.
Tendency toward neutrality in Uruguay fomented by failure of Allies to come to treaty agreement.
Inquires what action has been taken by Germany regarding protests against Belgian deportations.
Instructions to deny press report that the President will send second peace note to the powers.
Instructions to arrange for American inspection of work places of deported Belgians.
Presents German justification of system of deportation of Belgians.
Treatment of armed merchant ships as warships. Enclosure: Cipher message on subject for transmission to Berlin.
Declines to transmit to Germany Ambassador’s cipher message on offensive armament of merchant ships.
German policy of submarine attack on all armed ships without warning.

Quotes German note of Jan. 11 on sinking of Norwegian steamer Trippel.
From the German Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs to the American Ambassador
Sinking of the Norwegian S.S. Lökken.
Quotes German counter-reply to Allies’ rejection of Central powers’ invitation to discuss peace.
Quotes German note of Jan. 11 on sinking of Norwegian S.S. Lökken.
Requests authorization to appoint certain German consular officers to take the place of Bopp and Schack.
From the German Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs to the American Ambassador
Sinking of the British S.S. Barbara.
Press summary on armament of merchantmen and German determination to use submarines

Press summary of debate in the Prussian Lower House on unrestrained submarine warfare.

Inquiry whether any Americans among prisoners on board Yarrowdale.
Revocation of exequatur of Consul General Bopp.
Provisional recognition accorded new assignments of German consular officers at San Francisco and Seattle.
Inquiry regarding status of negotiations relative to submarine attacks on merchant vessels without warning.

Reported American prisoners are on Yarrowdale and German Government undecided what position to take regarding them.

No change of policy regarding armed merchantmen.

American citizens were among crews brought in by the Yarrowdale.

Discussion of German memorandum on armed merchant vessels.
Employment of reckless submarine warfare and blockade of English coast.
